title: Europe still isn’t ready for grey zone warfare
gist: Chatham House argues Europe is under an intensifying, coordinated grey zone campaign led by Russia (probing NATO Article 5 and Ukraine support) and Iran (intensified after US-Israeli strikes in February 2026), yet responses remain cautious and disjointed. Attribution alone (Estonia, France, Germany) is insufficient; governments must harden critical infrastructure and build public awareness — only 40% of Britons see Russia as a major threat beyond Ukraine — to win political will for defence spending.

themes.theme: Escalating Russian and Iranian grey zone campaign in Europe

insights.claim: Russia and Iran, Europe's primary adversaries, are increasing both the intensity and frequency of grey zone attacks across the UK and Europe, with recent incidents including spoiled food and fires in France, a botched drone attack at Leipzig Airport and bomb-threat flight groundings in the UK and across the continent.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect a continuing stream of sabotage, cyber and hoax disruptions to European transport, retail and infrastructure as a background risk.
insights.quote: As Europe’s adversaries – primarily Russia and Iran – increase the intensity and frequency of their grey zone attacks, national governments have been cautious and disjointed in their response.
insights.locator: As Europe’s adversaries – primarily Russia and Iran

insights.claim: The UK Ministry of Defence defines grey zone or 'sub-threshold' attacks as those that do not usually meet the legal definition of an act of war, covering election interference, disinformation, cyberattacks, sabotage, drone harassment and manufactured security hoaxes.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Frames which disruption types (cyber, sabotage, hoaxes) to monitor as state-linked rather than random events.
insights.quote: The UK Ministry of Defence defines grey zone, or ‘sub-threshold,’ attacks as those which do not usually meet the legal definition of an act of war.
insights.locator: Not quite war, not quite peace

insights.claim: Russian grey zone attacks on European states have increased since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while Iran significantly intensified its European grey zone efforts after the US and Israel launched strikes against it in late February 2026.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Middle East conflict has added a second state actor to European hybrid-threat risk since early 2026.
insights.quote: Iran significantly intensified its grey zone efforts in Europe after the US and Israel launched strikes against it in late February 2026.

insights.claim: China, North Korea and non-state actors such as cybercrime syndicates have also previously been accused of grey zone tactics across Europe, beyond the main Russian and Iranian threat.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The threat set is broader than Russia and Iran, widening cyber-risk exposure for European infrastructure.

themes.theme: Strategic aims of grey zone warfare

insights.claim: Grey zone warfare appeals because it lets perpetrators sow confusion and disunity, trigger critical infrastructure failures and gain strategic advantage without full-blown armed conflict, while straining government resources, dividing public opinion and weakening international cooperation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Attacks target cohesion and policy support as much as physical assets; political fragmentation is the intended outcome.
insights.quote: The appeal of grey zone warfare lies in the ability of perpetrators to sow confusion and disunity among targeted populations and trigger failure in critical infrastructure systems
insights.locator: The appeal of grey zone warfare lies

insights.claim: European governments see Russia's grey zone attacks as aimed at hampering their support for Ukraine, and Russia is likely testing European NATO allies' capacity to absorb aggression without triggering NATO's Article 5 mutual defence provisions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Below-threshold probing of Article 5 is an escalation-risk signal for European defence and security pricing.
insights.quote: Russia is also likely testing European NATO allies’ capacity to absorb grey zone aggression without triggering its Article 5 mutual defence provisions.

insights.claim: Tehran likely aims to disincentivise Europe from aligning with US and Israeli Middle East policy and is less likely than Russia to intend its grey zone attacks as the instigation of outright conflict.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Iranian activity is coercive signalling rather than a precursor to war, implying lower escalation risk than Russian activity.
insights.quote: Tehran likely aims to disincentivise Europe from aligning with US and Israeli foreign policy objectives in the Middle East

themes.theme: Europe's cautious, fragmented response and attribution

insights.claim: European governments have struggled to respond to grey zone activity in a way that deters future attacks, because such attacks fall short of explicit acts of war, are hard to attribute immediately and mimic natural disruptions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Absence of deterrence implies attack frequency is likely to keep rising.
insights.quote: They usually fall short of explicit acts of war, are difficult to immediately attribute to perpetrators, and mimic natural disruptions.

insights.claim: Some states are attributing attacks publicly: Estonia opened court proceedings against Russian saboteurs who allegedly attempted arson against a UAV manufacturer on 14 November, France named Iran's Revolutionary Guards for the October 2026 supermarket refrigerator hacks, and Germany blamed Russia for the failed August 2026 Leipzig Airport bomb attack.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Defence manufacturers (e.g. drone makers) and retail/cold-chain systems are named targets.
insights.quote: France has named Iran’s Revolutionary Guards as responsible for the October 2026 supermarket refrigerator hacks.
insights.locator: For example, Estonia has already publicly

insights.claim: Officials are framing the situation as neither war nor peace: Germany insisted it is 'not at war' while expecting similar attacks, and the commander of the UK's Cyber and Specialist Operations Command said the UK is not 'at war, but we're not at peace either.'
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: UK Cyber and Specialist Operations Command
insights.so_what: Governments are signalling a prolonged sub-threshold conflict state rather than a transient episode.
insights.quote: the UK is not ‘at war, but we’re not at peace either.’
insights.locator: Germany, too, was quick to identify Russia

insights.claim: Attribution of individual attacks without wider public awareness of sustained Russian and Iranian campaigns risks the public misreading them as one-off incidents; without public support for resilience measures, Europe will remain limited to clandestine, reactive and disjointed responses.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Policy response depends on public framing; watch for governments shifting to explicit 'coordinated attack' messaging.
insights.quote: Europe should acknowledge that it is effectively under coordinated attack and communicate this publicly.
insights.locator: Attribution of recent attacks is helpful

insights.claim: Governments need to take more preventive steps to protect obvious vulnerabilities: Poland's army was tasked in December 2025 to protect key energy infrastructure, and the UK's proactive identification of a cybersecurity flaw after the freezer hacks enabled a cross-sector awareness campaign that prevented a similar hack.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Rising state demand for infrastructure security and cyber resilience, particularly in energy.
insights.quote: Poland’s army, for example, was tasked in December 2025 to protect key energy infrastructure.

insights.claim: Preventive measures carry costs: dedicating military forces to protect infrastructure could impede frontline readiness.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Trade-off between homeland protection and expeditionary capacity shapes defence budget allocation.
insights.quote: dedicating military forces to protect infrastructure could impede frontline readiness.

themes.theme: Political will and the West-East divide

insights.claim: Western European governments find it harder than Eastern European countries closer to Russia to build political will for proactive defence, fearing moves seen as initiating unnecessary conflict or raising defence spending amid cost-of-living concerns; in September 2026 only 40 per cent of British residents surveyed by YouGov saw Russia as a major threat to Europe beyond Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Low threat perception in the UK constrains defence-spending increases versus Eastern Europe.
insights.quote: In September 2026, for example, only 40 per cent of British residents surveyed by YouGov thought Russia posed a major threat to Europe beyond Ukraine.
insights.locator: It is also harder for Western European

insights.claim: To build political will, governments should invest in awareness campaigns, via verifiable and credible outlets, that explicitly connect separate attacks domestically and transnationally, and could draw on civil society efforts such as the Sahaidachnyi Security Center's sub-threshold warfare tracker.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Public awareness campaigns are a leading indicator of future grey zone defence spending.
insights.quote: Awareness efforts also must go beyond individual attack attribution and explicitly connect various separate attacks, both domestically and transnationally.

insights.claim: Greater public awareness could support higher defence spending for a two-pronged approach of aid to Ukraine plus tailored infrastructure security, which may be less expensive overall than exclusively rearming national militaries for a future conflict.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Suggests a spending mix tilted toward infrastructure security and resilience rather than only conventional rearmament.
insights.quote: Financially, this might also be less expensive overall than exclusively focusing on rearming national militaries for a future conflict.
insights.locator: Increasing public awareness of what is at stake

insights.claim: Without a forward-looking, unified approach, Europe risks giving Russia, Iran and other aggressors the upper hand in any future conflict escalation; the risks of inaction far outweigh the costs of acting now.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Author sees escalation risk as asymmetric to Europe's downside absent coordinated action.
insights.quote: The risks of inaction far outweigh any costs of acting now.
insights.locator: Without a more forward-looking and unified approach
